Artist Turns Y2K Nostalgia Into Glossy 3D Objects That Make Old Technology Feel More Futuristic Than Ever

9

ad
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 1:05
Instaread

SAY!, a Ukrainian 3D motion and brand-identity artist whose practice turns nostalgia into glossy, animated digital objects. Drawing on the visual language of 1990s and 2000s consumer culture — keychains, MiniDiscs, charms, toy packaging, chrome logotypes, and cult media references — the work makes familiar artifacts feel newly collectible and alive.

SAY! uses cultural references as raw visual material rather than nostalgia for its own sake. A 3D remake of the Neon Genesis Evangelion logotype, for example, reinterprets an iconic wordmark as polished, dimensional type. The MiniDisc work similarly treats obsolete technology not as a dead format, but as a tiny “metal ritual” — an object whose physical design still carries a strong feeling of futurism.

This is why the work feels contemporary despite its references. It recognizes that the objects people remember are not only useful products; they are containers for rituals, private taste, personal identity, and the eras that shaped how people first learned to love design.
